metaTitle: Ticks in New Hampshire: Types, Lyme Map, Season
metaDescription: Deer ticks live in all 10 New Hampshire counties, and residents had 1,573 Lyme cases in 2023. Tick photos, a county Lyme map, the season and tick ID help.
h1: Ticks in New Hampshire: Species, County Maps, Lyme Data and Tick Season
dek: Which ticks live in New Hampshire, where Lyme disease is most common county by county, when each tick is active, and where to get a tick identified or tested.
excerpt: Deer ticks are established in all 10 New Hampshire counties. Species photos, Lyme rates by county, tick season by month and the state's free tick ID service.

quickAnswer.lead: **Blacklegged (deer) ticks and American dog ticks live in all 10 New Hampshire counties, and the deer tick spreads all five tick-borne illnesses found in the state.** Residents reported 1,573 Lyme disease cases in 2023, a rate of 113.4 per 100,000 that ranked seventh among states, according to [CDC surveillance data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/surveillance-data-1.html). The state's own count reached 1,806 in 2025.
bullets: CDC lists blacklegged ticks as established in all 10 counties through December 2025, and the germs behind Lyme disease, anaplasmosis and babesiosis have been found in host-seeking ticks in every one of them.
Relative to population, 2023 Lyme rates were highest in Sullivan, Grafton and Cheshire counties along the Connecticut River and lowest in Coos County, based on CDC county counts and Census estimates.

The state says ticks are active whenever it is above 40°F with no snow cover and most active from April through November; UNH's fact sheet says adult deer ticks are most active from early October to late November and from late March through May.
CDC counted 16 Powassan virus cases in New Hampshire residents from 2004 through 2025, 11 of them from 2023 to 2025.
As of October 2026, the state Department of Agriculture identifies ticks free for residents and UNH Extension tests them for a fee, but CDC generally does not recommend tick testing.
CDC's low Lyme counts for 2014 to 2016 and 2020 to 2021 are far below the state's own estimates for those years, which ranged from 1,027 to 1,563 cases.

body.text: Which ticks live in New Hampshire?

Mostly two: the blacklegged tick, often called the deer tick, and the American dog tick, both found in every county. UNH Extension's [fact sheet on New Hampshire ticks](https://extension.unh.edu/resource/biology-and-management-ticks-new-hampshire-fact-sheet), whose survey map dates from November 2017, called the dog tick the one people meet most often and said the blacklegged tick might soon overtake it.

The blacklegged tick matters most for health. The state health department's [tickborne disease page](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/programs-services/disease-prevention/infectious-disease-control/tickborne-diseases) lists five tick-borne illnesses in New Hampshire, Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, *Borrelia miyamotoi* infection and Powassan virus, and says the blacklegged tick spreads all five. Ehrlichiosis, tularemia and Rocky Mountain spotted fever, it adds, can be caught when traveling to other parts of the country, including other New England states.

body.text: Dog ticks are bigger and patterned: UNH puts an adult at about 1/8 inch long, brown and tan with an obvious mottled back, and a fully fed female at almost the size of a dime. The Lyme bacterium has been found in dog ticks, but UNH says tests show they cannot pass it on. For sizes and markings side by side, see [how to tell the common US ticks apart](/blog/what-do-ticks-look-like).

body.alt: Adult female American dog tick on a blade of grass, reddish-brown with a cream and white mottled shield behind the head and pale-banded legs
body.caption: Adult female American dog tick. Its pale, mottled shield sets it apart from the plain dark shield of a deer tick.
body.credit: CDC/DVBID/ Gary O. Maupin; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: Do winter ticks and woodchuck ticks bite people?

Winter ticks rarely do. UNH says this tick completes its whole development on one large animal, often a moose, deer or horse, from fall to spring, does not commonly bite people and does not transmit agents that cause disease in people. Hunters in the woods in October and November sometimes sit or put a hand on a cluster of its larvae, and as many as 50 have been found on a glove or pant leg afterward. Its real toll is on moose: heavy infestations sometimes kill them, and UNH reports New Hampshire research showing winter ticks limiting the moose population, with especially high calf deaths. More in the [winter tick guide](/blog/winter-tick).

body.alt: Adult winter tick seen from above on a white surface, with reddish-brown legs and an oval back patterned in cream and dark brown
body.caption: An adult winter tick. UNH says adults look like slightly elongated American dog ticks.
body.credit: (c) Megan Dark, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: The woodchuck, or groundhog, tick lives in every county and is commonly found on small and medium-sized mammals and on people. It does not spread Lyme disease, but UNH notes that it is a vector of Powassan virus, a rare and serious infection first found in New Hampshire in Hillsborough County in 2013. See the [groundhog tick guide](/blog/groundhog-tick) for how to recognize it.

body.alt: Engorged groundhog (woodchuck) tick on a wooden surface, its swollen body pale gray behind a small dark reddish-brown shield, head and legs
body.caption: An engorged woodchuck tick, also called the groundhog tick.
body.credit: (c) adamfritz, some rights reserved (CC BY), via iNaturalist

body.text: Has the Asian longhorned tick reached New Hampshire?

Not as an established population. USDA's [national situation report](https://tickapp.tamu.edu/invasive-ticks/asian-longhorned-tick-situation-report/) of December 4, 2025, lists infested counties in 25 states and Washington, D.C., including Maine, Massachusetts and New York, but none in New Hampshire or Vermont. The state's free identification service, described below, can name any tick you do not recognize, and the [Asian longhorned tick guide](/blog/asian-longhorned-tick) shows what to look for.
Where are deer ticks found in New Hampshire?

In every county. [CDC's county surveillance table](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/tick-surveillance-data-sets.html), which runs through December 31, 2025, lists blacklegged ticks as established in all 10, meaning six or more ticks of one life stage, or more than one life stage, were collected in a county within 12 months. CDC credits the listing of Coos County, at the northern tip, to data submitted in 2023; the other nine rest on older records. To compare other states, see [tick maps and Lyme data for every state](/learn/ticks-by-state).

They are not spread evenly. UNH's fact sheet found them most abundant in the southeast: about 85% of the population was within 35 miles of the coast in 2007, and 67% of its survey data points were within 40 miles in 2015. In the west, numbers were higher near the Connecticut River than farther away. UNH cautions that its map leans toward places near the university, where more people submit ticks.
Which germs have been found in New Hampshire ticks?

The germs behind Lyme disease, anaplasmosis and babesiosis have been found in host-seeking blacklegged ticks, meaning ticks looking for a host rather than feeding on one, in all 10 counties, according to CDC's companion pathogen table.

body.title: Germs found in host-seeking blacklegged ticks by county, New Hampshire, through 2025

Lyme, anaplasmosis, babesiosis and B. miyamotoi

body.caption: Germs identified, by species-specific molecular tests, in blacklegged ticks collected while seeking a host. The record is cumulative and depends on how much each county has been sampled and tested, so a germ missing from a county is not proof it is absent there. Anaplasmosis means the human-active variant of *Anaplasma phagocytophilum*. CDC credits both Powassan virus records to 2025 data.
body.source: [CDC ArboNET Tick Module (county status through Dec 31, 2025)](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/tick-surveillance-data-sets.html)

body.text: How many ticks carry the Lyme germ? The state's latest figures are more than a decade old. UNH reports that in state health department sampling, nearly 60% of adult blacklegged ticks carried *Borrelia burgdorferi* in 2007 to 2010, and the share stayed close to 60% in 2013 and 2014. For what that means for a single bite, see [what share of ticks carry Lyme disease](/blog/what-percentage-of-ticks-carry-lyme-disease).
Is the lone star tick in New Hampshire?

Only rarely, and the records are thin. [CDC's lone star tick surveillance](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/data-research/facts-stats/lone-star-tick-surveillance.html), which runs through 2025, lists the tick as established in Merrimack County and reported in Rockingham County, with no record elsewhere; no record does not mean no ticks. CDC's data file credits both entries to published literature rather than surveillance data, and notes that the Rockingham record, from a 2014 compilation, was a tick removed from a person, a kind of record CDC no longer uses because the person's travel history may be unknown.

CDC defines established the same way for lone star ticks as for deer ticks, and keeps the status in later years. UNH's fact sheet, whose map dates from 2017, describes a rare visitor: lone star ticks rarely turn up in the state, and it is unclear whether those found survived the winter or hitchhiked from farther south. They cannot spread Lyme disease but are the main carrier of ehrlichiosis, which the state lists among infections that can be caught when traveling; UNH says the 28 cases reported in New Hampshire from 2010 through 2014 were most likely linked to travel. The [lone star tick guide](/blog/lone-star-tick) shows how to recognize one.
How much Lyme disease does New Hampshire have?

New Hampshire residents reported 1,573 Lyme disease cases in 2023, according to [CDC's Lyme disease surveillance data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/surveillance-data-1.html). That count ranked 13th among states, but relative to population New Hampshire ranked seventh, at 113.4 cases per 100,000 residents, behind Rhode Island, Vermont, Maine, West Virginia, Massachusetts and Pennsylvania.

body.caption: Confirmed and probable cases. CDC's figures run through 2023, its latest year as of October 2026; 2024 and 2025 are state counts (the state's 2023 count, 1,574, is one more than CDC's). For the lows of 2014 to 2016 and 2020 to 2021, the state itself estimated more than 1,000 cases a year (see the table below). A revised case definition took effect in 2022, so later years are not directly comparable, and CDC says COVID-19 left 2019 and 2020 data incomplete in some states.

body.text: Why are some years so low?

Mostly because of how cases were counted. Staffing vacancies and eliminated positions left the state unable to investigate suspected cases reported in 2014, 2015 and 2016, its [2011 to 2016 Lyme report](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/sites/g/files/ehbemt476/files/documents/2021-12/lymecounty2016.pdf) explains, so it estimated those years from the reports received and historical data. Its [2017 to 2021 report](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/sites/g/files/ehbemt476/files/documents2/lymecounty-2017-2021.pdf) estimated 2020 and 2021 the same way. CDC's figures sit far below those estimates:

Cases in CDC's data

body.caption: State estimates from its reports dated July 25, 2017, and November 7, 2022. The state's current monthly report lists 401 cases for 2021 and calls that year's Lyme surveillance incomplete.

body.text: A second break came in 2022, when a revised national case definition let high-incidence states such as New Hampshire report cases on laboratory evidence alone. [CDC's report on the change](https://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/volumes/73/wr/mm7306a1.htm) says cases in high-incidence states rose 72.9% in 2022 over their 2017 to 2019 average, likely because of the new method rather than a change in risk, and that the changes rule out detailed comparisons with earlier years. New Hampshire did not jump: its 1,085 cases in 2022 were below its 2017 to 2019 average of about 1,506 (BuzzSkito's calculation from CDC data).

The state's [monthly infectious disease report](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/sites/g/files/ehbemt476/files/documents2/inf-diseasereport-monthly.pdf), dated September 28, 2026, carries the count forward: 1,496 cases in 2024 and 1,806 in 2025, the most in its 2021 to 2025 table, plus 418 for 2026 through August 31, a partial year. It last updated full-year totals on February 25, 2026, and says its 2020 to 2023 data must be interpreted with caution because pandemic-era effects on health care and reporting are not fully understood.
How does New Hampshire compare with its neighbors?
All three of its neighbors had higher Lyme rates in 2023, and the rates in Vermont and Maine were nearly twice New Hampshire's.

body.text: Which New Hampshire counties have the most Lyme disease?

Relative to population, the western counties along the Connecticut River. In 2023, Sullivan County recorded about 202 Lyme cases per 100,000 residents, followed by Grafton (about 160) and Cheshire (about 155), while Coos County in the far north had the lowest rate, 32. The map shows every county's 2023 rate, calculated by BuzzSkito from [CDC's county-level Lyme data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/lyme-disease-case-map.html) and the [Census Bureau's county population estimates](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-counties-total.html).

body.title: Lyme disease cases per 100,000 residents by county, New Hampshire, 2023
body.caption: Confirmed and probable cases by county of residence. Rates are BuzzSkito's calculation: CDC's 2023 county counts divided by the Census Bureau's July 1, 2023 estimates (Vintage 2025). CDC's file places 1,564 of the state's 1,573 cases in a county; calculated this way, the statewide rate is 111.6, close to CDC's 113.4. Coos County's 10 cases came from about 31,000 residents, so its rate can swing sharply.
body.source: [CDC county-level Lyme disease data](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/lyme-disease-case-map.html), 2023; [U.S. Census Bureau county population estimates](https://www.census.gov/data/tables/time-series/demo/popest/2020s-counties-total.html)

body.text: Raw counts follow population instead. Hillsborough County, the most populous, had the most cases in 2023 (410), followed by Rockingham (259) and Merrimack (227), yet Hillsborough's and Rockingham's rates were below the statewide figure.

The burden has shifted west and north. In 2008, Hillsborough, Rockingham and Strafford counties had 87% of the cases CDC could place in a county; in 2023 they had 54%, though home to about 63% of residents. Cases in Cheshire, Coos, Grafton and Sullivan counties rose from 70 to 367 over the same years. These are BuzzSkito's calculations from CDC county counts and Census estimates; case definitions changed in between, so the shift in shares says more than the raw totals.

Two cautions apply. Cases are counted where patients live, not necessarily where they were bitten, as [CDC's case map page](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/data-research/facts-stats/lyme-disease-case-map.html) notes. And small counties swing fast: in Sullivan County, with about 44,000 residents, each additional case adds more than 2 per 100,000 to the rate.
Which other tick-borne diseases occur in New Hampshire?

Anaplasmosis and babesiosis, both spread by the blacklegged tick, come next. The state's [monthly report](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/sites/g/files/ehbemt476/files/documents2/inf-diseasereport-monthly.pdf) counted 276 anaplasmosis cases and 57 babesiosis cases in 2025, but it flags its surveillance for both as incomplete in 2024 and 2025, so neither year can be read as a decline.

head: Disease
2026, through Aug. 31
body.caption: State counts by the date closest to the start of illness, from the [monthly report](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/sites/g/files/ehbemt476/files/documents2/inf-diseasereport-monthly.pdf) dated September 28, 2026; 2026 data were complete as of September 25. Ehrlichiosis includes undetermined *Ehrlichia* or *Anaplasma* infections. No tularemia was reported from 2021 through August 2026. State counts may not match CDC's.

body.text: Ehrlichiosis and spotted fever stay rare, in line with the state's description of them as infections that can be caught when traveling. For symptoms and treatment, see the guides to [anaplasmosis](/blog/anaplasmosis) and [babesiosis](/blog/babesiosis).
How common is Powassan virus in New Hampshire?

Rare, but more frequent lately. [CDC's Powassan virus data](https://www.cdc.gov/powassan/data-maps/historic-data.html), finalized on September 16, 2026, count 16 cases in New Hampshire residents from 2004 through 2025, all of them neuroinvasive, meaning the virus reached the brain or the membranes around it: one each in 2013, 2016 and 2017, two in 2019, four in 2023, three in 2024 and four in 2025. The state's monthly report also lists a 2021 case that is not in CDC's file, and two cases in 2026 through August 31.

CDC's [Powassan symptoms page](https://www.cdc.gov/powassan/signs-symptoms/index.html) says many infected people never feel sick, but about 1 in 10 people with severe illness die, about half of survivors have lasting health problems, and no medicine treats the infection. In ticks, CDC's pathogen table credits both New Hampshire records of the virus, from Rockingham and Strafford counties, to 2025 data. The [Powassan virus guide](/blog/powassan-virus) has more on symptoms.
When is tick season in New Hampshire?

Any day above 40°F without snow cover, with the most activity from April through November. That is how the state health department's [tickborne disease page](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/programs-services/disease-prevention/infectious-disease-control/tickborne-diseases) puts it, adding that exposure can happen year-round and that blacklegged nymphs, the stage most likely to give people a tick-borne disease, are most active from late spring through summer, most often May through August.

body.text: UNH's fact sheet says most Lyme infections in the state are picked up from late May through mid-July, when nymphs are out, and that nymphs cause most human cases because they are small and easily overlooked. Adults return in fall, so keep checking for ticks after the leaves turn. See [when tick season starts and ends across the US](/blog/tick-season).
Where can you get a tick identified or tested in New Hampshire?

As of October 2026, the state identifies ticks free but does not test them: the health department says the Department of Agriculture, Markets and Food identifies ticks for free for New Hampshire residents, to map where each species lives, and does not test them for any disease. The department's [identification page](https://www.agriculture.nh.gov/farms-businesses/plant-industry/pest-identifications/insects-spiders-and-ticks) says its entomologists work under a microscope or from a reasonably sharp photo sent with its online form, though photos and ticks missing their mouthparts may be identified only to genus. To send a tick:

items: Make sure it is dead; if not, put it in the freezer for a day.
Place it in a vial or other crush-proof container; ticks crushed in the mail or covered in tape cannot be identified.
Fill out the department's tick identification form.

Mail both to the NH Department of Agriculture, Markets and Food, Division of Plant Industry, State Lab Building, 29 Hazen Drive, Concord, NH 03301, or leave them in its drop box at the Health and Human Services building in Concord.

body.text: For testing, UNH Extension's [tick testing service](https://extension.unh.edu/tick-testing) charges a fee for each tick and emails results as early as 3 days after the lab receives it. Blacklegged and other *Ixodes* ticks are tested for *Borrelia burgdorferi*, *Borrelia miyamotoi*, *Anaplasma phagocytophilum*, *Babesia microti* and Powassan virus; dog ticks and other species for *Ehrlichia muris*, *Francisella tularensis*, *Rickettsia rickettsii* and Powassan virus.

Use a result with care. The UNH page tells anyone with medical issues to consult a medical professional, and CDC's [after-a-bite guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/after-a-tick-bite/index.html) generally does not recommend tick testing. CDC says results should not be used for treatment decisions, a positive tick does not prove you were infected, a negative one can falsely reassure someone bitten by another, infected tick, and treatment for someone who becomes ill should not wait for a result.
What should you do after a tick bite in New Hampshire?

Remove the tick right away, without waiting to see a provider, then watch for a rash or fever. [CDC's after-a-bite guidance](https://www.cdc.gov/ticks/after-a-tick-bite/index.html) describes removal this way:

items: Grasp the tick as close to the skin's surface as possible with clean, fine-tipped tweezers.
Pull it away from the skin with steady, even pressure, without twisting or jerking. If mouthparts stay behind and will not come out easily, leave them; the skin will push them out as it heals.
Do not use petroleum jelly, heat, nail polish or other substances to make the tick let go.
Clean the bite and your hands with soap and water, rubbing alcohol or hand sanitizer, and never crush a tick with your fingers.

body.text: The [step-by-step tick removal guide](/blog/how-to-remove-tick-safely) covers the details, and [a full-body tick check](/blog/how-to-do-a-tick-check) shows where ticks hide.

Speed matters. In most cases a tick must be attached for more than 24 hours before it can transmit the Lyme bacterium, and removing it within 24 hours greatly reduces the chance of Lyme disease, according to CDC's page on [how Lyme disease spreads](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/causes/index.html). The state health department adds that other tick-borne diseases can spread with shorter attachment times.

New Hampshire is one of the high-incidence states for Lyme disease, and CDC's [Lyme prevention page](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/prevention/index.html) says a single dose of the antibiotic doxycycline after a tick bite in an area where Lyme disease is common may, in certain circumstances, lower the risk of Lyme disease. It advises asking your healthcare provider whether antibiotics after a tick bite are appropriate for you.

Then watch for symptoms. CDC's [Lyme symptoms page](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/signs-symptoms/index.html) says early signs appear 3 to 30 days after a bite: fever, chills, headache, fatigue, muscle and joint aches and swollen lymph nodes, with or without a rash. The erythema migrans rash occurs in about 70% to 80% of infected people, begins at the bite after about 7 days on average, expands over several days to 12 inches or more across, may feel warm but is rarely itchy or painful, and sometimes clears into a bull's-eye. A small bump or redness that appears right away at a bite, like a mosquito bite, is common. [The stages of Lyme disease symptoms](/blog/lyme-disease-symptoms-guide) explains what can follow untreated infection.

body.alt: Expanding red rash with a darker red center and a paler outer ring on the back of a person's upper arm, the erythema migrans rash of early Lyme disease
body.caption: Erythema migrans, the expanding rash of early Lyme disease, in a bull's-eye pattern. CDC says the rash sometimes, but not always, clears into this shape.
body.credit: CDC/ James Gathany; photo: James Gathany (CDC Public Health Image Library, phil.cdc.gov)

body.text: The state health department advises watching for signs and symptoms of tick-borne disease for 30 days after a bite and contacting a healthcare provider if symptoms develop. CDC says to see a doctor if you develop a rash or fever within several weeks of removing a tick, and to say when the bite happened and where you most likely picked up the tick.

body.title: See a healthcare provider if you feel ill
body.text: A rash or fever in the weeks after a tick bite is a reason to see a provider and mention the tick. Do not wait for a tick test result. This page summarizes what public health agencies publish and is not a diagnosis.
How do you prevent tick bites in New Hampshire?

Cover up, use repellent, treat clothing with permethrin and check for ticks every day. The state health department's [tickborne disease page](https://www.dhhs.nh.gov/programs-services/disease-prevention/infectious-disease-control/tickborne-diseases) recommends these steps:

items: **Dress for ticks.** Wear light-colored clothes that cover your arms and legs, and tuck your pants into your socks before heading into wooded or grassy areas.

**Put repellent on exposed skin.** The state suggests 20% to 30% DEET; CDC also lists picaridin, IR3535, oil of lemon eucalyptus, para-menthane-diol and 2-undecanone among EPA-registered options. Follow the label.

**Use permethrin on clothing, not skin.** The state calls permethrin highly effective at repelling ticks on clothing and says it is not meant for skin; CDC recommends clothing and gear treated with 0.5% permethrin.
**Stay on the path.** Avoid tick-infested areas when you can and keep away from brush; the state says outdoor workers in New Hampshire are at particular risk.

**Check, shower and dry.** Check for ticks daily, especially behind the knees and ears, in the groin and belly button, and on the back and neck; shower soon after coming indoors; and dry clothes on high heat for 10 minutes, or an hour if they are wet or damp.
**Protect pets.** Check pets for ticks daily and ask a veterinarian about tick preventives; [the guide to ticks on dogs](/blog/ticks-on-dogs) shows where to look.

body.text: Around the house, CDC's [prevention page](https://www.cdc.gov/lyme/prevention/index.html) suggests a 3-foot-wide barrier of wood chips or gravel between lawns and wooded areas, keeping grass mowed, removing leaf litter and clearing tall grasses and brush.

faqs.question: Are ticks active in New Hampshire in the winter?
faqs.answer: Yes, on mild days. The New Hampshire Department of Health and Human Services says ticks are active any time the temperature is above 40 degrees Fahrenheit and they are not covered by snow, and that exposure can happen year-round, although ticks are most active from April through November. UNH Extension says adult deer ticks keep seeking hosts in mild winter weather when there is no snow cover, so check for ticks after time in woods or brush even in December or March.

faqs.question: Which New Hampshire county has the most Lyme disease?
faqs.answer: It depends on whether you count cases or rates. Hillsborough County had the most cases in 2023, 410, because so many people live there. Relative to population, Sullivan County was highest at about 202 cases per 100,000 residents, followed by Grafton and Cheshire counties, while Coos County was lowest, based on CDC county counts and Census estimates. Cases are counted where patients live, not where they were bitten, and small counties can swing sharply from year to year.

faqs.question: Can I get a tick tested for Lyme disease in New Hampshire?
faqs.answer: Yes, but not by the state. As of October 2026, the state Department of Agriculture, Markets and Food identifies ticks free for residents but does not test them, while UNH Extension tests ticks for the Lyme bacterium and other germs for a fee. CDC generally does not recommend tick testing, because a positive tick does not prove infection and a negative result can falsely reassure. If you feel ill after a bite, see a healthcare provider rather than waiting for a result.

faqs.question: Why do New Hampshire's Lyme numbers drop in some years?
faqs.answer: Mostly because of how cases were counted. Staffing vacancies left the state unable to investigate suspected cases reported in 2014, 2015 and 2016, and it estimated 2020 and 2021 from the reports it received and historical data, so CDC's counts for those years are far below the state's estimates. A revised case definition took effect in 2022, letting high-incidence states count cases on laboratory evidence alone, so recent years are not directly comparable with earlier ones.

faqs.question: Are lone star ticks in New Hampshire?
faqs.answer: Rarely. CDC's surveillance data list the lone star tick as established in Merrimack County and reported in Rockingham County, but both records come from published literature, and the Rockingham one was a tick removed from a person. UNH Extension's fact sheet, whose map dates from 2017, says the tick rarely turns up in the state and may hitchhike from farther south. Lone star ticks do not spread Lyme disease, though they can spread ehrlichiosis, which the state lists among infections that can be caught when traveling.

faqs.question: How long does a tick have to be attached to spread Lyme disease?
faqs.answer: Usually more than 24 hours, according to CDC, which says removing a tick within 24 hours greatly reduces the chance of Lyme disease. The New Hampshire health department adds that other tick-borne diseases can spread with shorter attachment, so remove any tick right away with fine-tipped tweezers. CDC also says that in certain circumstances a single dose of doxycycline after a bite in an area where Lyme disease is common may lower the risk; ask a healthcare provider whether it is right for you.
